speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our country is facing a highly uncertain future.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even jobs that were traditionally performed by workers physically onsite may no longer be ring-fenced from foreign competition.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We read of blue-collar work like coal mining in Henan, China can now be done by 5G technology, where workers remotely operate excavators deep underground in the air-conditioned comfort of their homes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our path to recovery will be long and steep.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In spite of the dire situation, Singapore can still emerge richer in other ways.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Government has done much to help fellow Singaporeans to save jobs and provide emergency support to workers and companies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But there is other help that is needed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In times of scarcity, it is natural that we look out for our own needs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But history has also shown us that it is in the darkest nights that the brightest stars shine.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My hope is that Singapore will be such a star.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this difficult time, we can all come out richer – richer as a nation in our civic-consciousness, kindness and graciousness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is time for everyone to chip in with whatever we have.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As a community, we have to take an interest in each other’s needs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to come together to help the vulnerable, and this is especially true for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is a topic that is close to my heart because of the older demographic in my Yio Chu Kang constituency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are three things that I feel we can do better as a community to help our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, we need to wrap help and care around seniors in the community.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our Government has many schemes and programmes already in place for seniors to ensure that they can age well in place.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We can certainly do more to wrap help around the seniors and to do this in the community, rather than to ask seniors to seek out schemes which are organised around agencies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some Government agencies have already begun doing this work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I know this because I was formerly in MOH looking after ageing planning policies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I also ran the Silver Generation Office (SGO).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We leverage volunteers who are Ambassadors to visit seniors in their homes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They also share with them Government schemes that specifically applies to their needs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is a good thing, as last-mile communications are important for this vulnerable population segment who may not know who to turn to.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am heartened to see that SG Digital Office (SDO) moving into the community to teach seniors how to use new technology, a space where there is still much more to do.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I was at the “Seniors Go Digital” event by SDO and IMDA at Teck Ghee Community Club last weekend.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I saw many enthusiastic seniors who were eager to learn new digital functions like e-payments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Talking to Mrs Tan, who is a grandmother at the event, she shared that she was excited that she had learnt how to connect with her grandchildren via Zoom.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: She asked me what else she can do online.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Speaking with her, it reaffirmed my belief that technology opens up many more possibilities when coupled with human care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should move decisively to have a one-stop online digital service centres for all things related to seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is no need for seniors to travel to a physical location just to look for help, and in this way, improve information and care referral.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should also endeavour to convert all Residents' Committee (RC) nodes into telehealth pods and get volunteers or part-time care aides from the community to assist seniors in their consultations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In introducing seniors to the use of telemedicine, they will be able have follow-up visits in the community without making the journey to the hospital.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In these ways, technology can help wrap services around our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, Government services and the assistance of our healthcare friends are not enough to help our seniors through this crisis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, we need to tackle loneliness through stronger community bonds.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have become lonelier as a society with COVID-19 and tele-commuting and we can expect a lot more empty nesters, singles and seniors living alone in the future.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Social isolation among older adults is a serious public health concern because of their heightened risk of physical and mental health problems.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is further exacerbated through the COVID crisis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A recent Lancet article recommended urgent action to mitigate the mental and physical health consequences for the elderly if they remain at home and avoid social contact during the crisis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Everything eventually falls back on the need for and the importance of relationships and social bonds.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am glad that some hon Members have also spoken about this.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Building strong social relationships is a complex issue but is something we need to do well in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Simple, everyday actions can also make a big impact.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I was heartened to hear about the story of Mr Toh who lives in Yio Chu Kang.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: During the circuit breaker period, Mr Toh called SGO after he realised that he did not see his neighbour, whom he knew was ill, coming out of her flat for a few days.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: SGO and the nearby Senior Activity Centre assessed the situation and called for an ambulance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mr Toh's neighbour was eventually admitted to hospital and was discharged a few days later.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If not for Mr Toh's timely actions and knowledge of his neighbour, she could have suffered greater consequences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need more Mr Tohs to build community and counter isolation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On a broader scale, we saw the community coming together to help others during the circuit breaker period, such as through food distribution to seniors living alone.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I believe we can do this well because we are a high-rise and compact community.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And many of us live next to each other.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Volunteers from outside the community can be helpful, but there is no substitute for neighbours looking out and caring for each other.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It creates a very different culture in the block and neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We can do more to expand and deepen the community network.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, as we have the community chipping in, we should use our different strengths to create a stronger society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Making a senior-friendly place is beyond infrastructural improvements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In helping each other, we must leverage on our various strengths and abilities to create a stronger social compact.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When one has ability, we should do our best to help others without the ability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When one has resources, one should share our resources with those in need.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If one is weak, we can look to those who are stronger to support us.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: During my house visits, I met people with differing resources and needs, like the uncle living alone in a rental flat, a single young mother who needs to raise five young kids, retirees who play chess at Block 610, professionals living in landed estates, even a former Minister who lives in the ward.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I continue to have residents who write to me to ask how they can volunteer for the community.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we match these resources to the people who need them within our communities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we should not "waste" a crisis by spending our time wishing we were out of it or reminiscing the past.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must live in the present and work for the future.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should have passion in the public discourse, to bring out creativity, be a catalyst for change and for our people to seek out new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But besides reflecting, we also need to act.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is much that we have to do together as a people.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Government cannot provide all the help to everybody.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There will not be enough time, not enough resources and not enough attention.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we need the whole nation to work together to meet the needs of every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is great value for us to do more for each other.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This can be a reset in our nation building journey.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We either react by fighting for ourselves or watch out for each other.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How we react will define us as a nation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As Singaporeans, we have gone through thick and thin together in the past.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yio Chu Kang was a big kampong area 50 years ago, a kampong of mainly coconut plantations and fresh fish farms.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I took the opportunity to speak with old residents who had stayed in Yio Chu Kang from the kampong days till today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They shared with me how neighbours would help each other in times of harvest, such as picking coconuts and gathering fish, because the tasks were too onerous for each family to carry out on their own.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One such resident, Mr Vincent Toh, recalled how he used to follow his father and uncle around the kampong in Lorong Lentor learning how to help his neighbours in these endeavours, often late into the night.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: During my walkabouts, I met Mr Peter Chong, who is a hawker selling chicken rice at our Yio Chu Kang 628 Food Centre.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A soft-spoken man, he offers discounted food to healthcare workers who he recognised through their uniforms.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He also looks out for the seniors who would at times forget to bring money for their meals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chong would let them to have their meals and pay him another time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such small daily acts of kindness and endearing moments are appreciated by the seniors and the Yio Chu Kang community.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is in the same spirit as SG Together, a shared conviction to work together and help each other to take Singapore forward.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In times of scarcity, we can be richer if we help each other.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Reach out to those in need in times of crisis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This need not only be in big ways but in our everyday actions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The year 2020 thus far has been a trying year for Singaporeans and life as we know it has changed in the span of just a few months.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Not forgetting my fellow educators, from the early childhood sector to the primary schools and secondary schools as well as to those in the IHLs, for facing our students every day and provide normalcy when times are rough.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Their dedication and ability to adapt underlie the quality of the educators that we have, and I hope that we can continue to provide them with the best support and work-life balance as possible.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I would also like to take this opportunity to wish a Happy Teachers’ Day in advance to all of them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: One key message from the President's Address that resonates strongly with me, and that I urge for the House to continually review, is in ensuring continuous social mobility in Singapore, especially through our education system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The recent Addendum by MOE to redouble their efforts to ensure that no child is left behind and to ensure multiple pathways to achieve success is much welcomed.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The standard route for many of us is that we go through the primary, then secondary schools before moving on to tertiary education either in the junior colleges, polytechnics or ITEs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Following this set mould, some would then attain a bachelor's degree, which is seen as the endpoint and pinnacle of one's education journey.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I would like us to continually challenge this notion, especially when we are serious about lifelong learning.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To sustain something lifelong requires us to understand how to prevent physical and psychological burnouts that may happen throughout this journey.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This may include providing opportunities for individuals to discover, rediscover and reinvent themselves.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe that lifelong learning should not be an extension of just the tertiary education, but also an extension on the other end, the Early Childhood education.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In this way, the education journey is spread over a longer period of time, reducing its intensity, yet at the same time, extending the runway for one to pursue their passion and making them invaluable experts in their chosen field.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A longer runway also implies that if one decides to change their field of interest or finds a new one, it is never too late.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Within this extended timeline, I would like to point out three key phases of interest.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We often hear the notion that children are like sponges, due to their ability to absorb information.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But this ability would not be maximised without the opportunity to play and explore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Through deliberate play and exploration, children discover skills of social interaction and problem-solving beyond what books can offer.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As you can see, the benefits of emphasising play during this critical juncture are long term.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By the time a child enters primary school at the age of seven, without a solid foundation during this critical window, it may be too late.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How often do we see our young children choosing mobile devices over physical activities?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The formation of ECDA and NIEC, programmes such as KidSTART and the increase in Government subsidies for preschools show that we are in the right direction towards making preschool accessible for all.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Currently, there are over 250 courses available in our local polytechnics and universities, allowing students to choose a course that matches their interest and passion.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, the collapse of certain sectors and the streamlining of the workforce brought upon by COVID-19 has exposed the inability of some of our fresh graduates to be agile in a volatile job environment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As an educator, I have met many ex-students from both the polytechnics and the universities who are unable to secure jobs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Some of them are my primary school students from 15 years ago.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A typical scenario would be a fresh graduate in a particular affected sector, who suddenly finds himself at a complete loss with the dismal state of his particular industry due to the specialised nature of his course.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This then raises the question of how specialised their education should be at this stage.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Because clearly, early specialisation constraints their skillsets and limits opportunities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, the next question may be when the specialised skills should be introduced.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am a strong believer that this should be done on-the-job.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As fresh graduates learn from the job and develop their passion and eventually specialise, it is at this juncture where they rediscover, as they enrol in specialised courses in the polytechnics or universities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I envision a future where such specialised courses are curated in collaboration with industry partners, creating a symbiotic relationship between content and relevance, and further supported by a robust apprenticeship approach.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Importantly, if a similar crisis were to strike again, we have done our part to ensure that every Singaporean graduate is future-ready and remains employable.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I recall my own struggles managing my work, my responsibilities as a young father, as well as studies and research.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The only perk that I could think of was that living in Punggol and travelling all the way to the Nanyang Technological University (NTU) meant that I had a lot of time to read my notes in the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT).

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Although I must admit, like any other adult learners who also have families and who reach home late, I usually end up using that time to catch up on sleep.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Support for adult learners requires work on multiple fronts.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It starts from building an employer culture that sees value and allows time for the employee for training and education.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The COVID-19 situation has proven to us that learning online is possible and it may be the preferred mode for future learning.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Personally, I have conducted numerous online lectures with adult learners who appreciate the flexibility, and the time saved from travelling.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Recently, I met a few individuals who have further inspired me in preparing this speech: Mr John Chong who, after 37 years in the Education Service as a teacher, Head of Department (HOD) and Vice Principal, pursued his passion to be a beekeeper; Mr Jabez Tan, a food and beverage (F&B) business owner who, despite going to prison five times, developed his passion for cooking, researched on the best "Bak Kut Teh" recipe and eventually became successful; and Mdm Narindarjeet Kaur, who has been a nurse for 40 years, her passion for her job motivated her to attain numerous certificates in her area of specialisation before attaining her degree at the age of 55.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Collectively, they have proven to me the importance of passion and the need for multiple starting points to achieve success.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay):   In my speech earlier, I highlighted the importance of education at the preschool level.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The age of four to seven is important in the development of children, it is the best time for them to gain knowledge and be given a strong foundation before entering primary school.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I would also like to take this opportunity to thank the mosque staff and religious teachers who have worked diligently to ensure that our society remains safe in the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our religious teachers have successfully recreated themselves through virtual conferencing and they continue to play an important role in guiding and advising the community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In this period of service, I hope to contribute further into the issue of social mobility through education, so that Singaporeans, regardless of age and their starting points, are always given the opportunity to improve their lives.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us renew our commitment towards building a better future for all Singaporeans, a future that we all help to build and, together, look forward to.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: (In Mandarin):   The sudden and unprecedented COVID-19 crisis has completely changed the global environment, economic activities as well as our lifestyles.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: More importantly, it has forced us to re-position ourselves under this new normal, and reconsider the mode of survival and thinking, in the context of country to country, people to people, and how people relate to themselves.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Fifty five years ago, when Singapore was forced to become independent, we were like an abandoned baby and no one expected this tiny country with its inherent inadequacies to survive miraculously.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Yes, it is the hard work and the wisdom of our forefathers that have made Singapore what it is today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We have limited land and our natural resources are even less, an innate condition that cannot be changed.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, these constraints did not stop our creativity from expanding.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Even without domestic flights, Changi Airport and Singapore Airlines have become world-renowned leaders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Of the world's largest container terminals, four out of the top five are in China which has a huge market.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Singapore, with its very minuscule market, managed to occupy a place among them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: COVID-19 has turned every country into an abandoned baby, and the world is facing a serious pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Drastic economic downturns and the challenges that follow have caused many people to complain or feel lost, anxious and even panic.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: History tells us that with each crisis, there will be some people who will be ruthlessly eliminated, but others will be able to clench their teeth and go against the tide.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They will find opportunities amidst the crisis and eventually emerge victorious by creating history.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Indeed, to survive, you must be brave enough to change.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Not long ago, K-pop boy band BTS held a virtual concert during the pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In this crisis, we have to face the key element of survival, and that is the change in the mindset.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Our people have to change; our businesses have to change; our Government has to change.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: What we have to do is to re-shape a new Singapore that is vibrant, full of opportunities, full of vitality and wisdom.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In this process, we need more synergies from the top to the bottom, and vice versa.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This includes tolerance, openness and support from the Government as well as trust, buy-in and participation from the people.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Only when the whole nation works together as co-creators can we overcome the difficulties together and once again create the next chapter for Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: (In English): As the world shut down and more people stayed at home in our battle against COVID-19, many people turned to the Internet for information, services and entertainment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Many of these online offerings tend to be available free of charge or supported by public funds.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The same problem faced by media companies for many years with a weak business model for online content still exists today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, a virtual concert streamed by K-pop boyband BTS in June turned out to be the world's largest paid online music event.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The 100-minute show allowed fans to enter and navigate through BTS’ virtual house, where they could choose close ups and full shots among six multi-view screens playing simultaneously and enjoy the group’s highly choreographed performance of 12 songs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: There were also intermission-type talk segments, similar to a physical concert.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The successful transformation from a conventional to an online concert calls for mind-set changes and innovation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The concert venue is like the environment and infrastructure provided by the government for companies to do business and for people to make a living and to lead their lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: With an economy built largely by MNC and enterprise investments, the Singapore workforce has for many years, been trained to find a good job, work hard for a promotion and salary rise, or change job when there is a better opportunity and higher pay.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: That is, to be an employee with a company.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I am glad and heartened that among its extensive range of assistance schemes to help businesses and people cope with the pandemic, the government came out with SIRS to specifically help self-employed persons – people who do not have a formal relationship with any employer.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In 2007, I spoke about the freelancers in the arts sector.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: While NTUC has stepped up to help administer the scheme, I hope the Government would proactively gather useful knowledge from NTUC’s experience on the many different ways that SEPs are operating.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Even before COVID-19, the gig economy has been growing.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: During and after the pandemic, there will be and have to be new ways to make an honest living, other than working for an employer.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Our rules and policies should not unnecessarily disadvantage people who are not in the formal employment that we are used to.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The Government will have to be nimbler in offering different “venues” so that “virtual concerts and other new formats” could be staged.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The stadium might have to be "broken up into smaller modular spaces".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In terms of Government policies, I hope we can take a look at the CPF system.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: It was set up to help build financial adequacy for citizens in retirement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Over the decades, it has become intertwined with financial provisions for housing, healthcare and education.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: It has become a very complicated system that many people unfortunately do not understand the full benefits.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Once, a resident wanted to appeal for early withdrawal from her Retirement Account (RA) to settle some personal loans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: She was honest enough to tell me that, actually, she has savings in a fixed deposit account.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But she did not want to touch it because she does not want to lose the interest.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: So, when I shared with her that she is actually getting up to 6% interest in her RA which is probably much higher than what the bank would pay her, she immediately changed her mind.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The CPF has been built around an employer-employee model where both parties contribute a part.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, SEPs do not have any employer and most do not make their own contribution except maybe for their MediSave.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They may not even be captured in our system or be counted in any statistics.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Unlike employees of a company, they also do not have HR or Finance departments to help them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: As a commercial entity, whether MNC, SME, social enterprise or sole proprietorship, its primary objective has to be sustainable and profitable.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But when the industry, technology or consumer preferences change, the business model has to evolve.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For example, the music industry has gone through and survived the vinyl record, cassette tape and CD eras into digital music.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To supplement the lower revenue from digital music, singers and musicians have to do live performances and concerts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, it is unlikely that large scale concerts will be resumed anytime soon.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: So, the BTS concert example demonstrated that an online concert can be commercially viable, too.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Good news for BTS fans, they have announced an "offline and online" concert in October and, this time, there will be some limited seating for live audience.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: So, they are also not sitting on laurels and are now moving on with a new formula.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Certainly, talent, showmanship and popularity are key to their success.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But it is also the willingness and out-of-the-box thinking to reformat the concert that made it possible, to be accessible and profitable, probably more so than a physical concert.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Hence, I urge businesses to seriously think about their own future in a different world.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: By all means, make good use of the Government’s help to stay afloat and retain your staff.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But if a business is surviving just because of the Government’s help, it is probably not going to last very long.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Businessmen and entrepreneurs have the natural instinct to adapt and to sniff out new opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This is what the commercial world is good in, and that is not the forte of the Government.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The Government can help by being open and supportive, or even more open and more supportive, and we should not stand in the way for new and creative ways of doing and trying out business.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: As consumers and members of the public, we must also do our part in a different world.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: While there were netizens who complained about needing to pay for the BTS concert, many fans who tuned in found that it was really worth the price.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For a fraction of what they used to pay, they can get up close and enjoy a different experience watching their idols.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Of course, they must accept that the screen on their device cannot compare with the set-up in a concert venue.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In a stadium, audience can enjoy the sound system, lighting effects, air-conditioning or even the refreshments sold there.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But when we are watching an online concert, it becomes our own responsibility to ensure that we have a conducive environment to enjoy the concert, and we cannot complain about it.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: So, in the new normal, when almost everyone is affected by the pandemic, we all share a common enemy.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We must stand united against this same enemy.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Each of us will have to do our part to get out of this crisis.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Recently, a netizen complained to me that it is not fair that he could not qualify for SIRS because his wife earned more than $70,000.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: He said that that is his wife’s money, not his.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Well, I understand for many couples or maybe some couples, the husband’s money belongs to the wife money, but the wife’s money is hers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But during difficult times, we should turn to our immediate family for help and support, especially if they have the means.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Over the last few months, we stayed at home more, spent more time with our family, and forged closer ties with our loved ones.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The skies have turned bluer, we see more rainbows and more wildlife around us.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Hopefully, we will be wiser to know what the truly important things are in our lives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many Members have already spoken about the need to mitigate the crippling effect of COVID-19 on our economy and our people during these challenging and unprecedented times.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am very heartened also that while the methods and the means might differ, that both sides of the House are united in the approach that we have to strengthen the Singapore Core and support Singaporeans through this difficult time.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What I would like to focus on is what Mdm President said in her Address last week with regard to how Singapore’s model of meritocracy has to evolve and change.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I find that we would need to move beyond too narrow a definition of meritocracy, especially vis-a-vis our education system.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened that in the speeches shared earlier by Minister Maliki and Minister of State Sun Xueling, they both stressed that we have to move away from the focus on the academic arena to move into other broader, non-academic arenas, as it were.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My point is to look at it from a slightly different perspective, Mdm Deputy Speaker, and that is to make the point that we have placed too much focus, not so much on academic qualifications per se, but on examination-based academics for too long.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our children and students are often judged by a grade or a mark that is determined by how well they are able to perform in an examination.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But, yet, there are many students who are not able to deliver an examination-based performance, but who are no less intelligent or capable than their peers who are able to do so.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I spent more than 16 years in the Polytechnic and worked with students who had less than stellar grades based on their examination-based academic results.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, when they were exposed to an academic system that was based more on coursework and project work, they were able to score well and achieved very good GPA; thus achieving, and I quote, “academic success”, albeit in a less examination-centric system.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, grades and GPA, Mdm Deputy Speaker, are important; they do give us some indication of how students perform.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I would hope that MOE can continue to work on how we can create more academic systems that are less examination-focused and more coursework based.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In short, let us work on different grading systems, broader grading systems, which allow different students different paths to achieving good grades.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recognise and applaud the fact that there already are alternative routes that students with differentiated intelligences and capabilities can take to move on into Secondary schools, such as the DSA.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also applaud the fact that MOE is moving towards PSLE scoring bands, as opposed to using absolute T-scores.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But the fact is that the PSLE still remains the “mother-of-all-examinations”, one that relies purely on students’ ability to replicate what they have learnt over the years in a few hours.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And if we look at it, Mdm Deputy Speaker, what does a PSLE score tell us?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What the true potential of that child is?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Or is it simply a snapshot of how well that child can be drilled to take an examination at a particular point of their life?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am not suggesting that the PSLE be scrapped any time soon.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is no indication of what one can truly achieve.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In moving beyond traditional definitions of success, we have the opportunity to redefine what "great" looks like, looking further past academic achievements and to those who have not only walked roads less travelled to the beat of their own drum, but achieved the highest standards in their chosen field.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is not just about celebrating mavericks per se, but mastery of a chosen field by those whose efforts merit recognition and reward for their unrelenting pursuit of excellence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the culinary scene, our Singaporean chefs regularly take home Gold at top international competitions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the 2016 Culinary Olympics which are held once every four years, Louis Tay, Teo Yeow Sian, Tristan Fang, Alan Wong, Roy Lim and Alex Chong took on the best in Germany and the world and they came out tops.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, I wonder if more can be done to celebrate our Singaporean gastronomical rock-stars in the same way that we herald the international chefs cooking in Singapore’s kitchens.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, why not extend the definition of excellence in the arts to beyond the classical?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And if we do have someone who is able to make a mark for Singapore on the international stage in the performing arts and raise the profile of our country – for example, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng talked about BTS, the Korean phenomenon, although I must admit I am more of a Blackpink fan myself, thanks to and purely because of my daughter, nothing else – I would love it if, one day, we had a Singapore pop phenomenon who succeeds at the global level, we should celebrate and promote this achievement because they have brought the Singaporean brand name to a global international level.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have a chance now, as a collective society, to recognise merit across a broader level and this can only make for a richer and more diverse representation of who we are as Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My grandmother, who is now 92, used to make my sister and I quilts when we were much younger.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Coming from the tough, hardy Pioneer Generation, my grandmother did not believe in wasting money on new blankets and made these quilts from various scraps of cloths that were sewn together.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of these cloths had more of some prints than others; some were leftovers from a blouse, or even excess scraps from pyjamas – all were unique, none were the same.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes, the prints clashed, sometimes they were complementary.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The quilt kept us warm when we needed it; at other times, it was a pretty reminder of my grandmother’s love because, as my sister just reminded me recently, quilting is hard work.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Which is why in some cultures, quilting is a real communal activity – many hands make light of hard work.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And when there is a tear, everyone comes together to mend the fabric.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a sense, I think of the Singapore identity as a quilt.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The metaphor is quite similar, although I think, in the Minister's term, the tapestry is something more grand and majestic, which I also see Singapore as.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The reason why I picked the quilt is because the quilt, for me, is something that you hold close to you, it keeps you warm, gives you comfort and protects you.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our Singapore identity as a quilt is a patchwork of many cultures and multiple identities that we have stitched together and that has stayed together over the past 55 years.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But, like any quilt, over time, we do have the occasional tears in the fabric, too, and some parts of our quilt maybe they are fraying at the edges.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And only if we are able to do so with kindness.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: After all, if we start to turn on each other and start to be unkind – if we flame, criticise, destroy, tear down, burn down rather than build, construct and work together, then we begin to rip the quilt apart.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We have witnessed how an intertwined unprecedented economic and health crisis has affected our lives.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Those who understand that this is going to be the new normal are preparing themselves for the rough journey ahead.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In this pandemic, it is now more imperative than ever to push on with our continuous efforts to create a robust and inclusive education system for our children and youths.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: From a young age, parents, family and teachers heaped praises on our young ones, to encourage them to be the very best they can be.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Every parent wants the best for their children and push them towards their own notion of success.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: When these children grow up, many become fixated on this notion of easy success and they want it and want it quickly.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our education system is exemplary when it comes to imparting knowledge and skills for the future economy.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Yet, given how fluid and competitive today's economy is, all these will come to nought if our youths are incapable of reacting well to changes and setbacks.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Just before the pandemic hit us, I spoke about resilience in individuals and as a nation in the first Budget speech of 2020.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Resilience is a critical skill that all educators, both at home and in school, should impart.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some of the methods to incorporate resilience in the classroom include discussions and reflections on goal-setting and perseverance, sharing stories of success and failures, understanding strengths and weaknesses through student-led report cards.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Our education system has been evolving in this direction, reducing the emphasis on academic results and nurturing talent across different arenas.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I hope more can be done to expose students to more experiences that will encourage resilience and perseverance in our children and youths.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The job market was bleak and we could not see the glorious rainbow that we were looking forward to.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But the mountain tops also have valleys in between.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is in these "valley" moments that we grew more robust, more determined and resilient, and soar out of these valleys.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I read with interest in the Straits times in April of fresh graduates facing lower salaries and rejections, and I reminisced about our days in 1998.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Then, my NUS friends and I sent out hundreds of job applications, too, and we had low starting pay.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Thankfully, MOE was recruiting teachers, and some took up the offers, yet some others became administrative staff.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As for me, I studied insurance and did real estate work.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She worked hard and did a part-time ACCA.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I saw articles of graduates' concerns of low starting pay affecting their future earning power.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I say to them, "Do not worry about this.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Go out there, learn and gain experience, even if it is not your field of study.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: You will gain other useful skills, such as teamwork, communication and planning skills, that will pay dividends well into your future." Those of us in this House that do yoga or pilates will be familiar with a pose called the "plank." It is a simple exercise similar to a push-up position.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: You support your body with your elbows and your back in a straight line to your ankles.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It holds you upright and improves your stability and core strength for the next time you need to sprint.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Perseverance and resilience are our society's core muscles.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Like all workouts, you cannot do it with just one repetition and expect results.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It requires a quiet determination to push forward through the pain, uncertainty and ambiguity.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We need to have faith in our family who provide our hearts inspiration, encouragement from our friends, and trust that our Government will leave no one behind.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I want to encourage all those seeking jobs not to wait for a better job with less work and more pay.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Instead, look at investing in yourself, build your toolkit with new skills, grow your library of experiences.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Develop a strong core of perseverance and resilience, and I promise you, when we are out of this valley, it will be your time to soar.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Yesterday, we heard the Prime Minister remind us that this is possible due to the hard work and sacrifice of our founding generations.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He called the reserves our rainy day money or coffin money.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I know many people and businesses are struggling in these tough times.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I met some residents, a couple, who were staying in a 5-room flat.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Their children had married and moved out to their own flats.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They were not on talking terms with their children.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They even had a Court Maintenance Order to require their children to support them.
